cases.description: Microsoft's documented breaking-strength example: population variance of ten numeric readings
cases.expected_note: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 678.84 (the same page shows VAR over the same data as 754.27). Independently derived: mean = 13286/10 = 1328.6, sum of squared deviations = 6788.4, divided by n = 10 (population denominator) = 678.84

cases.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a text cell is counted as the value 0 and included in n
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's VARPA page states 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)' (and, contradictorily, that range text is ignored -- resolved the same way as AVERAGEA's worked example resolves it). Under the counts-as-0 reading data become 1, 2, 3, 0 with mean 1.5; squared deviations 0.25+0.25+2.25+2.25 = 5, divided by n = 4 gives 1.25. An engine using VAR.P semantics on this range would return 0.6667 instead

cases.description: TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0 inside a range
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents 'Arguments that contain TRUE evaluate as 1; arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0' for VARPA: data 1, 0, 0 with mean 1/3; squared deviations (2/3)^2 + (1/3)^2 + (1/3)^2 = 2/3, divided by n = 3 gives 0.22222... -> 0.2222

cases.description: Population variance of a single data point is defined (0), unlike sample variance
cases.expected_note: The population denominator is n, not n-1, so one data point gives 0/1 = 0 rather than a division-by-zero error

cases.description: With no data points at all there is nothing to divide by
cases.expected_note: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's VARPA page documents NO error condition at all. Empty cells are documented as ignored, so an all-empty range leaves n = 0 and the population denominator is zero; #DIV/0! is the consistent result
